title: OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens Poses 'Unacceptable Risk,' Nonprofit Says
source_used: The Verge (the WSJ original, pool link, is blocked: HTTP 401)
key_facts: Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that reviews apps and services for youth safety, said that OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens is an 'unacceptable risk' (7 Oct 2026).
ChatGPT for Teens was introduced in August and has guardrails designed to help students learn.
The assessment found the product 'doesn't send alerts to parents when it should', does not give the right help in crisis situations, and 'still does kids' homework'.
Common Sense Media says the teen protections 'fall short of what the company promised'.
OpenAI disputes the findings and says the bulk of the testing may have begun and ended before parental controls were fully active.
Common Sense Media replies that some test accounts were linked for significantly longer and still got no notifications, so it stands by its conclusion.
quote_evidence: ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don’t work,
We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media’s testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice
why_it_matters_hint: Parents may rely on crisis alerts that the watchdog says often fail, and OpenAI disputes the test method.
notes: The Verge wrote its own report with statements from OpenAI and Common Sense Media, so The Verge is the source printed. The WSJ headline (pool) is the same assessment; WSJ page not readable. Read in full from the Verge page.
